'''''Spinifex sericeus''''', commonly known as '''hairy spinifex''', '''rolling spinifex''', '''beach spinifex''' or '''coastal spinifex''', is a [[Dioecy|dioecious]] [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[grass]].

It is native to [[Australia]], [[New Zealand]], [[New Caledonia]], and [[Tonga]].

It is an important [[pioneer species]] which colonises coastal [[dune]]s, binding loose sand with its horizontal runners.<ref name=rbgsyd>{{cite web |url= http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Spinifex~sericeus |title=''Spinifex sericeus'' R.Br.|access-date=2012-05-29 |work=PlantNET |first1= S. W. L. |last1=Jacobs |first2=Hastings |last2=S. M. |publisher=National Herbarium of NSW, Sydney }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Coastal Plants of the Bellarine Peninsula |author1=Longmore, Sue |author2=Smithyman, Steve |author3=Crawley, Matt |name-list-style=amp |year=2010 |publisher= Bellarine Catchment Network }}</ref>

The 1889 book ''The Useful Native Plants of Australia'' records that common names included "Spring Rolling Grass" and that it "has no claim whatever as a food plant for stock, and can only be recommended as a sand-binder in fixing drift sands when encroaching on valuable land. For this purpose it deserves more attention than has hitherto been bestowed upon it. It is a plant of comparatively rapid growth, and would give effectual aid in checking the inroads of wind-driven sand, conditionally that the plants be carefully conserved from fire."<ref>{{cite book | author=J. H. Maiden | year=1889 | title=The useful native plants of Australia : Including Tasmania | publisher= Turner and Henderson, Sydney | url= https://books.google.com/books?id=PHoxAQAAMAAJ&dq=useful+native+plants+of+Australia+hirsutus&pg=PA108 |page=108}}</ref>

==Description==
''Spinifex sericeus'' has branched [[stolon]]s and [[rhizome]]s extending up to {{convert|1|-|2|m|ft}}.  The leaves have a [[ligule]] of a rim of dense hairs; the blades are flat and densely silky.<ref name=rbgsyd/>

The male [[inflorescence]] is an orange-brown terminal cluster of spiky [[raceme]]s subtended by silky [[bract]]s.  The female inflorescence detaches at maturity, a globose seed head of [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]] racemes up to 20 cm in diameter which becomes a [[tumbleweed]].<ref name=rbgsyd/>
